title: The flute player in the rice fields
translation: A very young man came out through a shabby gate of woven bamboo. In the moonlight I couldn't make out the colours, but his silk jacket had a sheen to it, his trousers were dark, and he looked like someone of real breeding. With just one small boy for company, he set off down a long, narrow path through the rice fields, brushing through the plants and getting wet with dew. As he walked, he played the flute, beautifully, just for himself.

Nobody out here would know how good that is, I thought. I wanted to see where he was going, so I followed him at a distance. He stopped playing and went in through a big gate at the foot of the hills. Inside stood a carriage with the ox unhitched, and out here that caught my eye more than it would have in the city. I asked a servant, who said: "Prince So-and-so is staying here just now. I think there's some kind of Buddhist service."

Priests had gathered at the chapel. The scent of incense drifted over on the cold night wind and went right through me. The ladies-in-waiting walking along the corridor from the main house to the chapel were careful about the scent they left in the air behind them, even out here in a mountain village where nobody would see.

The autumn fields had grown just as they liked and were buried in more dew than they could hold. The insects sounded as if they were complaining, and the garden stream ran on quietly. The clouds seemed to cross the sky faster than they do in the city, and the moon kept coming out and going in again.

literal: From inside a humble woven-bamboo door, a very young man, the colours not clear in the moonlight, but in a glossy hunting robe and dark trousers, looking very refined, taking along one small boy, went along the narrow path through the distant fields, getting soaked by the dew on the rice leaves as he pushed through, playing the flute exquisitely for his own pleasure;

I thought there would be no one here to hear it and know it as moving, and wanting to know where he was going, I followed, watching him, and he stopped playing the flute and went in at a place with a main gate at the edge of the hills.

A carriage set on its stand could be seen, which caught the eye more than in the capital, and when I asked a servant, he said, 'It is a time when Prince So-and-so is staying here, and there is probably a Buddhist service or the like.'
Priests had come to the chapel.
The scent of incense burning out of sight, carried on the cold night wind, also felt as if it sank into me.
The ladies-in-waiting going from the main hall to the corridor of the chapel took care with the scent on the following wind and the like, not saying 'it is a mountain village where no one sees'.
The autumn fields, grown thick as they pleased, were buried in overflowing dew, the voices of the insects sounded reproachful, and the sound of the garden stream was calm.
Compared with the sky of the capital, the coming and going of the clouds seemed fast, and it was hard to tell whether the moon was clear or clouded.

notes.text: {狩衣|かりぎぬ}: originally a hunting robe, by Kenkō's time the everyday outdoor dress of a nobleman. {指貫|さしぬき}: wide trousers tied at the ankle. 'Glossy' means fine silk. Even in the dark, he is clearly not a farmer.

notes.quote: 笛をえならず吹きすさびたる
notes.text: え … ならず: 'indescribably, exquisitely' (literally 'cannot be (ordinary)'). すさぶ: 'to do something for one's own pleasure'. He is not playing for anyone.

notes.quote: あはれと聞き知るべき人もあらじ
notes.text: じ: negative guess, 'there will be no one'. Kenkō, of course, is there, listening.
{榻|しぢ}: a stand for the shafts of an ox carriage when the ox is unhitched. A parked carriage of a noble, out in the countryside.
{宮|みや}: a prince or princess of the imperial family. The servant gives the name; Kenkō replaces it with しかじか, 'so-and-so'. The text does not say whether it was a man or a woman.
{空薫物|そらだきもの}: incense burned somewhere out of sight, so that the scent seems to come from nowhere (see section 8 on incense).
{追風|おひかぜ}: the breeze that follows someone and carries the scent of their robes. {用意|ようい}: 'care, attention'. The ladies make sure they leave a good scent behind them, with nobody there to notice.

notes.quote: 虫の音かごとがましく
notes.text: かごとがまし: 'as if complaining, reproachful'. Insects in autumn were a standard sound of sadness in poetry.

notes.quote: 月の晴れ曇ること定めがたし
notes.text: The section ends with no comment at all, just the sky. The scene reads like one from the Tale of Genji: court manners, far out in the countryside.
